title: School Notebooks 5-pack

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: At same price ($9.03), median sales were 13 vs baseline 7.6 → x1.71, but noise-adjusted is x1.16. Thus, effective demand impact is x0.86 (1/1.16), so -14%.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery risk
drivers.evidence: Planner note warns of short delivery. No past data, but plausible to suppress sales. Downside effect shrunk due to uncertainty.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 7.6. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price increased by 2.3% to $9.03, which is above regular price. Historical data shows that at $9.03 (same price), sales were 10–16 units (median 13), vs baseline 7.6 — a 72% uplift, but noise-adjusted effect is x1.16. This suggests price increase suppresses demand. The supplier warning of short delivery implies supply risk, which may reduce available stock and thus sales. The classical model suggests no uplift, but judgment overrides it: a price increase with no promotion and a supply risk should lower demand. The noise-adjusted price effect is x0.86 (1/1.16), and supply risk adds downside. Combined multiplicatively and shrunk toward 1.0 due to thin evidence.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 9.03 (+2.3% vs regular price 8.83)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 7.6 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 42.1 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 26.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-64% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
